issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. Being alone with women is not a plausible primary trigger for partner violence in a female patient unless there is additional trauma history not represented elsewhere, and military/police uniforms also suggest a different threat context that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: The memory/appraisal pattern centers on guilt and global identity damage, but the selected triggers point toward external threat cues unrelated to intimate-partner violence. This creates a cross-node mismatch: the triggers imply one trauma context, while memory and appraisals imply another.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is not impossible, but in this profile it intensifies the mismatch because the appraisals are extremely global and identity-based while the trigger content is narrow and externally themed in ways not linked to the romantic-partner abuse formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: Military or police uniforms are not impossible as triggers after intimate partner physical abuse, but in this profile they are hard to justify because no other trigger, memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy item links the trauma to police/military involvement, authority figures, or uniformed responders. This makes the trigger feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
issues.explanation: This item is not impossible, but alongside the more specific interpersonal/self-related profile (self-blame, guilt on recall, being alone with men, body-focused avoidance, belonging nowhere), a global 'completely destroyed' worldview reads broader than the rest of the node and may overstate the appraisal pattern relative to the otherwise relationship- and self-focused presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reflects fear, hypervigilance, avoidance, mistrust, and tension after intimate partner physical abuse. It pulls toward a more disinhibited presentation that is not supported by the trigger, memory, appraisal, or other strategy items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Own Body' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The selected triggers, memories, threats, and appraisals center on interpersonal danger, guilt, and mistrust rather than body-focused trauma responses. This item is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the main formulation compared with the other avoidance item.

vignette:
Leilani is a 20-year-old married interior designer who came to treatment several months after a pattern of physical assaults by her husband had culminated in a night she now experiences as both vivid and strangely unreachable. During an argument in their apartment, he had cornered her in a dark hallway, shouting inches from her face before hitting her. What remains most charged for her is not a complete story she can tell from beginning to end, but fragments tied to sensation: his voice suddenly getting louder, the feeling of being trapped with a man between her and the exit, the sight of him afterward as if danger were still attached to his body. Those details make her present triggers feel immediately understandable. A slammed door in a client’s home, a male contractor lingering with her in a room, or unexpectedly seeing her husband can pull her back into the same state before she has time to think.

Since then, loud noises and being alone with men do not just upset Leilani; they push her into ways of managing that have steadily narrowed her life. If a site visit requires walking through a dim unfinished space, she finds a reason to stay near the entrance or asks someone else to check measurements. At work she avoids being alone in a room or building, timing her movements so she is always near a receptionist, assistant, or another designer. When something sets her off, she goes over and over what she must have done wrong, blaming herself for staying, for not seeing it coming, for not leaving sooner. The same triggers also bring an immediate bodily alarm. A dropped sample book or raised male voice leaves her superalert, shoulders tight, heart racing, scanning the room and then glancing behind her as if someone might be coming up on her. Just as quickly, these moments stir the memory system that troubles her most: she may suddenly feel the whole emotional force of that night without any clear picture, or she tries to describe what happened and loses the thread, overcome by guilt as she speaks.

Those trigger moments also seem to confirm what she has come to believe about herself and the world. When she freezes around male clients or feels herself recoil at seeing her husband, she thinks, with a kind of finality, that her life has been destroyed by what happened. She feels cut off from other people her age and from the person she was before, as though she no longer belongs anywhere. Underneath that is a hard mistrust: people cannot be trusted, especially when they appear calm and familiar.

These beliefs keep her body in a constant state of preparedness. Because she is certain that people are unsafe and that she is no longer protected by ordinary closeness, she enters most spaces already on guard. She sits facing doors, checks behind her in parking garages and hallways, and notices every shift in tone from men on job sites. The same beliefs shape the way she remembers. When she tries to put the assaults into words, the account collapses into guilt-laden fragments; it is as if her mind returns not to a coherent narrative but to a conclusion that she was foolish, damaged, and abandoned from any place of safety.

Her memories in turn drive much of what she does to cope. When the emotional intensity arrives without an image, she avoids dark rooms, avoids being alone in buildings, and tries not to be in circumstances that resemble that hallway. After any attempt to recall the abuse, she ruminates for hours about her own responsibility. The memories also intensify her sense of danger: after a fragment or bodily surge, she becomes even more watchful, more tense, more likely to turn around repeatedly. And because each incomplete recollection is saturated with guilt, it leaves her more convinced that the trauma has ruined her life, that she belongs nowhere, and that trust is naïve. In a cruel way, the memory itself has made the world easier to trigger; loud noises, male presence, and seeing the offender now feel linked to something unfinished and undefended inside her.

Over time, the strategies she relies on have made her world smaller and more threatening. Avoiding dim spaces and refusing to be alone in rooms at work have begun to affect her credibility as a designer, especially when projects require independent walkthroughs or meetings with male vendors. She has become preoccupied with arranging her day around perceived safety, and the constant self-blame leaves her feeling even more isolated and alien from others. The more she avoids, the less chance she has to learn that every dark room, every man, every sudden sound is not that night again; instead, each avoidance preserves the trigger. Her vigilance rises with this shrinking of her life, and the effort to stay safe has itself become exhausting.

Leilani finally sought help after having to leave a client meeting when a contractor dropped a metal ladder and the crash sent her into full-body panic. She could not explain to her supervisor what had happened; she started, lost the thread, and was overwhelmed by shame. What frightens her most is the sense that this is permanent—that she will always live braced for danger, unable to trust anyone, unable to feel at home anywhere. What she hopes, more quietly, is to be able to work, to enter a room by herself, and to remember what happened without feeling that the memory itself proves her life is over.
